items.title: Wendell Brunious interviewed by Michael Woods, Los Angeles, California, September 3, 1995 [interview 1 of 2]
items.q: when I first heard Charlie Parker and I go back to my Dixieland band and try and play like Charlie Parker

ctx.x: I do too. I didn’t know anything about improvising when I first heard these jazz records. I didn’t know they were making it up out of their heads. I just liked the music, you know. And then I remember hearing a Bix Beiderbecke record and reading all the critics or the writers you know they say the same thing. I think one guy reads something and then he recycles it you know. But everything I read about Bix Beiderbecke, they said he was fond of ninths and thirteenths. I thought oh well, that’s nice. And then the…

eight, nine. Oh, that’s a ninth. Oh that’s a ninth. Oh, yeah. You know, light — 20 watt light bulb. Oh that’s what a ninth is. And I went nine, ten, eleven, twelve, thirteen, oh, that’s a thirteenth. Oh, yeah, I’ve heard him do that. And then of course, as I mentioned, when I first heard Charlie Parker and I go back to my Dixieland band and try and play like Charlie Parker. Well then every solo I played, I went immediately for the ninth. Ninth, ninth, ninth — Banjo players, “Aw, Dan.” MR: I don’t want to rush you…
Oh, the heck with it. We’ll just stay here, send out for pizza. Do you have anything to tell the camera?

items.title: Dan Barrett interviewed by Michael Woods, Los Angeles, California, September 3, 1995
items.q: I can love Charlie Parker as much as anybody, and yet maybe I’m not cut out to play like that

ctx.x: Well, remember I always wanted to play the trumpet and in recent years I’m starting to play more and more cornet actually. But I try to approach the trumpet, or I try to approach the trombone more like a trumpet. And Louis is my big hero actually. If I had to pick one it would be Louis. And then I don’t know who the second one would be you

know, I mean there are so many guys I love, but Louis is number one. And I keep thinking about him and I keep thinking about playing as simply as I can. And this may be something that comes with age. I remember when I was 15 trying to do everything under the sun. And I was about 18 when I heard my first Charlie Parker record and — well no I can’t say that, I guess I was in high school — and I just didn’t get it. I really didn’t get it. And some students then in college, they said, “Hey Dan, I hear you’re…

the first half of your career you spend trying to sound like other guys and then the second half, if you’re smart, you spend it trying not to sound like those guys. You’re just trying to find your own voice.
